newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Tension rises in Mostar as more Moslems evicted.
newsitem.headline: Tension rises in Mostar as more Moslems evicted.

text.p: Tension rose in the divided Bosnian city of Mostar on Wednesday as a Moslem family were evicted from their home and Croat soldiers harassed a United Nations police patrol, U.N. officials said on Thursday.

The incidents came the day after Western European Union police handed over powers to Moslem and Croat police and increased concern over the ability of local forces to maintain order in an ethnically split community.

A spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, Mans Nyberg, said Wednesday's eviction was the first since September although there had been 54 Moslem evictions from Croat-held west Mostar this year.
Moslems and Croats fought an 11-month war in 1993 as a side-show to the main conflict with Bosnian Serbs, which ended in a U.S.-brokered accord to form a federation in March 1994.
International officials and mediators have been trying to reunite Mostar ever since with little success.

"It would be a mistake to characterize Mostar as a place of sweetness and light where progress is made very easily," said Colum Murphy, spokesman for the international community's High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt.
West Mostar has gained notoriety as a criminal haven where gangster bosses view reintegration "bad for business".

"The UNHCR condems this latest incident which only confirms the impression that west Mostar is one of the worst municipalities in Bosnia-Hercegovina with regard to human rights and especially the situation for ethnic minorites," Nyberg told reporters on Thursday.
In a separate incident in west Mostar, an unarmed U.N. police patrol was harassed by Croat soldiers who injured a female U.N. officer from the patrol and damaged their vehicle.
The harassed patrol of the U.N. International Police Task Force (IPTF) took refuge in a nearby butcher's shop while Croat soldiers repeatedly rammed their vehicle with a truck.
NATO troops arrested one of the soldiers while others fled through a large crowd, Svensson said.
He said Croat civil and military police did nothing to prevent the incident. They reported later that the detained soldier was drunk.

NATO also reported that an unapproved parade of the Bosnian government army took place in Moslem-held Mostar on Tuesday, prompting NATO to impose a country-wide ban on all Bosnian army parades for an indefinite period.
In addition, a training ban was imposed on Bosnian army units belonging to the Mostar corps, Boudreau said.
The 58,000-strong NATO force in Bosnia is charged with ensuring the military provisions of the 1995 Dayton peace accord for Bosnia are implemented.
